# One Set of Results {#sec-results}

```{python}
#| label: results-setup
# The evaluation project's results, computed once by its own script (scripts/evaluation.py).
import math

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from scripts import evaluation as ev
from scripts.figures import ACCENT, MUTED, figsize, style
from scripts.prose import alt_text_holds, number_words, text_holds

S = ev.summary()
best = S["best_version"]
WORD = number_words()
seg = ev.segments()
ages = seg[(seg["factor"] == "age_band") & (seg["version"] == best)].set_index("segment")
jobs = seg[(seg["factor"] == "job") & (seg["version"] == best)].set_index("segment")
most, least = ages["share_called"].idxmax(), ages["share_called"].idxmin()
cal = ev.calibration()
cal_best = cal[cal["version"] == best]
gap = (cal["mean_predicted"] - cal["observed_rate"]).abs().groupby(cal["version"]).max()
oldest = min(S["releases"], key=lambda r: r["month"])["version"]
top = ev.percent(S["top_share"], 0)
calls_double = math.ceil(2 * S["top_share"] * S["test_rows"])
# The sentences below say: the band called most is also the band most likely to subscribe;
# the best release is also the best calibrated.
text_holds(ages["base_rate"].idxmax() == most, "the most-called age band's subscription rate")
text_holds(gap.idxmin() == best, "the best-calibrated release")
# The opening says, without numbers, that the called list leans towards some ages and that
# one group is called far more often than another.
text_holds(ages.loc[most, "share_called"] > 2 * S["top_share"] > 2 * ages.loc[least, "share_called"]
           and ages.loc[most, "share_called"] > 3 * ages.loc[least, "share_called"],
           "the opening's \"called far more often than another\"")
# The payoff (media/capture/eval_outputs.py, step card): the card's title, subtitle and section 2.
import re

CARD = (ev.PROJECT.parents[1] / "checkpoints" / "15-eval-results" / "model-card.qmd").read_text()
alt_text_holds(dict(re.findall(r'^(title|subtitle): "(.*)"$', CARD, re.M)) == {
    "title": "Model card: contact-ranking model", "subtitle": "Acme Signals (a fictional company)"}
    and re.findall(r"^## (.+?) \{#", CARD, re.M)[1] == "Intended use", "fig-results-card")
# Every prompt in this chapter was dry-run, verbatim, by Claude Code (Opus 5.5) in a copy of
# checkpoint 14 on 2026-11-18; the traps in @tbl-results-traps and the story in
# @sec-results-change are the ones that run met. The model-card prompt was trimmed on
# 2026-11-25 (PLAN-improvement-briefs-2.md, D3), its nine section names moved out of the
# fence; the lead dry-runs the trimmed text.
```

The fast path ended with one report and one winner. This chapter asks a second question of
the same results: whom does the winning release call? The answer is in a file the report
never opened. The list the
call centre would work from leans towards some ages: one group is called far more often than
another. A report can leave that out. A model card cannot, and
writing one is this chapter's larger task: handed to the agent whole, with a plan first and
its checks after.

The design that answers it is the one the repository already has: **one script computes every
result once, and every document reads them**, so the card, the report and everything after
them quote the same run.

- Number sections and refer to them, to tables and to figures, so that every reference
  resolves in HTML, Word and PDF.

## Compute once, check three ways {#sec-results-checks}

`scripts/evaluate.py` is the only code in the repository that fits a model. It writes five
plain files to `outputs/`, the same bytes on every run in the environment `uv.lock` pins,
because every random choice, the split, the models and the bootstrap, has a fixed seed. In
this book's run the best release is `{python} best`, measured on `{python} f"{S['test_rows']:,}"` test contacts, of whom
`{python} ev.percent(S["base_rate"])` subscribed (the *base rate*):

| File | Holds |
|---|---|
| `summary.json` | the best release, test-set size, base rate, seeds and versions |
| `metrics.csv` | each release's metrics, with bootstrap intervals |
| `segments.csv` | the same by age band and by job |
| `calibration.csv` | predicted against observed rates, in `{python} WORD[cal_best["bin"].nunique()]` bins |
| `curves.csv` | the ROC and precision-recall curves |

: What the evaluation writes. {#tbl-results-outputs}

The metrics are *ROC AUC*, the probability that a release ranks a random subscriber above a
random non-subscriber, and three for the top of the list: *recall*, the share of subscribers
the calls reach (calling the top `{python} ev.percent(S["top_share"], 0)` at random would reach
`{python} ev.percent(S["top_share"], 0)` of them); *precision*, the share of calls that reach
one; and *lift*, precision over the *base rate*, the share of all contacts who subscribe. A metric's *bootstrap interval* is the range that holds the middle
`{python} ev.percent(S["confidence"], 0)` of its values when the test set is re-drawn, with
replacement, many times. Three kinds of check guard different things, and a repository
needs all three:

| Check | Runs | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| **Tests** (`uv run pytest`) | on the code and the data | a changed data file (its checksum); a leak |
| **Guards** (`claim(…)` in a document) | when a document renders | a sentence the results no longer support |
| **The render** | on every document, in every format | a reference that does not resolve; a failed cell |

: Three kinds of check, and what each catches. {#tbl-results-check-kinds}

A *checksum* is a fingerprint of a file: change one byte of the data, and it no longer
matches. A test does not read prose, and a guard does not test code; neither notices a stale
typed label, which only a reader, or a prediction tested by a rebuild (@sec-results-change),
will.

::: think
The data have a column, `duration`, the length of each call in seconds. The dataset's own
page, quoted in `data/README.md`, says it "highly affects the output target". Should a release
use it?

No. A call's length is known only after the call, and the model's job is to choose whom to
call. A model given it would be evaluated on something it can never have in service: a
*leak*, a column that carries the answer into the evaluation. No render would notice; a test
does (`tests/test_models.py`), which is why the repository has one.
:::

## A model card, as one larger task {#sec-model-card}

A *model card* is a short document that travels with a model: what it is, what it is for and
not for, how it performs overall and for the groups it affects, and what its makers know is
wrong with it. Mitchell and colleagues proposed the form in 2019, with a fixed list of
sections, which is the vocabulary to ask for.

The card is a good example of a task to hand over whole (@sec-step-or-task): you can state
the result (those sections, from those files), and its checks run without you (guards, the
references, the render). So ask for a plan first, read it, and only then let the agent work.
Start a branch for it, as for any change you will review:

::: {.you}
```bash
git switch -c model-card
```
:::

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
Plan first, and wait for my go-ahead: add model-card.qmd for the best release, with the sections of Mitchell et al. (2019). Read only outputs/ and data/README.md; age and job slices come from outputs/segments.csv, calibration from outputs/calibration.csv. Cite the paper and the dataset from a new references.bib, opening each DOI first. Guard every sentence whose wording depends on the results with `claim`. Render it to html, docx and typst, then list what you could not verify.
```
:::

::: {.agent}
replies with a plan · after your go-ahead: writes `references.bib` and `model-card.qmd` · `uv run quarto render model-card.qmd`
:::

<!-- Dry-run 2026-11-25, verbatim, in a copy of checkpoint 14-eval-start with outputs/

The paper, "Model Cards for Model Reporting", has nine sections: model details, intended use,
factors, metrics, evaluation data, training data, quantitative analyses, ethical
considerations, and caveats and recommendations.
**Read the plan** against them, as a reviewer would. A good plan lists the sections in order,
says where each number comes from, names the *slices* (the results for each age band and each
job) and the figure, says how it will check the references, and computes labels such as "top
`{python} top`" from `outputs/` rather than typing them. If the plan misses something, say so
before it starts. Then reply `Go ahead.`

When it finishes, the checks are the ones the prompt asked for:

- **The guards.** Read every `claim(…)` in the file: each should state a sentence of the
  card, and its condition should compute that sentence from `outputs/`. A guard whose
  condition can never be false, such as a name read from the results compared with itself,
  protects nothing.
- **The references.** `references.bib` should hold Mitchell et al. and the dataset, each with a
  DOI you can open. When this card was built, the dataset's DOI record had its authors
  garbled, and the agent cited the dataset as the repository's own page gives it: a reason to
  open DOIs, not only to collect them.
- **The list of what it could not verify**, the most useful part of a larger task's report:
  how the split was made, how the calibration bins were formed, that the ethics text is its
  own framing. Each item is a question for you, not a defect to accept.
- **The render.** Open the three formats, and look at the slices as their subjects would.

The finished card's slices make the point. Under `{python} best`, the
called top `{python} top` of the list holds `{python} ev.percent(ages.loc[most, "share_called"])`
of the contacts aged `{python} most` but `{python} ev.percent(ages.loc[least, "share_called"])`
of those aged `{python} least`. The ranking follows how often each band subscribes, and in
these data the `{python} most` band subscribes most often (`{python} ev.percent(ages.loc[most, "base_rate"])`).
That is accurate, and a card must say it. Age is a *protected characteristic* in UK law: the
Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination because of it. The data are a
Portuguese bank's, but the card asks for legal review before any UK deployment. A bank must
know before it relies on the ranking.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-results-ages
#| tbl-cap: "The best release's slices by age band, from the evaluation's outputs: the share of each band's contacts in the called list, the band's subscription rate, and the share of its subscribers the calls reach."
#| output: asis
lines = ["| Age band | Test contacts | Called | Subscription rate | Recall |", "|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|"]
for band, r in ages.iterrows():
    lines.append(f"| {band} | {int(r['n']):,} | {ev.percent(r['share_called'])} | "
                 f"{ev.percent(r['base_rate'])} | {ev.percent(r['recall_top10'])} |")
print("\n".join(lines))
```

| What you see | The fix |
|---|---|
| The first render stops: pandas' styled tables (`df.style`) need `jinja2` | write the table another way, rather than add a dependency |
| The PDF cites in another style, with a second "Bibliography" page | `citeproc: true` under `typst:` |
| An old `model-card.html` after a failed render | read the render's last lines before you open the file |

: Met while testing the card, 2026-11-18. {#tbl-results-traps}

## Sections, numbers and references {#sec-results-sections}

The report grows two sections, and a reader of a three-format document needs to find them.
Numbered sections and cross-references do that, and each is one setting or one label:

| You ask for | Quarto's feature | It renders as |
|---|---|---|
| numbered sections | `number-sections: true` | "2 Who is called" |
| a section referred to | `## Who is called {#sec-segments}` and `@sec-segments` | "Section 2", a link |
| a table or figure | a `tbl-` or `fig-` label, then `@tbl-…` | "Table 2", "Figure 2" |
| one citation style | `citeproc: true` for `typst` | "(Mitchell et al. 2019)" in all three |

: References, and the setting behind each. {#tbl-results-refs}

The check is in the prompt: an unresolved reference renders as "??", in every format.

::: {.prompt .long}
```default
In report.qmd, number the sections and add two: who is called (recall in the top 10% by age band, from outputs/segments.csv, as a table labelled `tbl-segments`) and calibration (a figure labelled `fig-calibration` from outputs/calibration.csv), each with a guard where its wording depends on the results, and refer to both from the opening paragraph with @sec- references. Render all three formats and check that no cross-reference shows "??".
```
:::

::: {.agent}
edits `report.qmd` · `uv run quarto render report.qmd`
:::

Calibration asks whether a predicted probability can be read as a rate: of the contacts the
model gives 20%, do about one in five subscribe? @fig-results-calibration draws it for the
best release.

```{python}
#| label: fig-results-calibration
#| fig-cap: "Calibration of the best release on the test contacts: the observed subscription rate against the mean predicted probability, in equal-sized bins. On the dashed diagonal, predictions equal rates."
#| fig-alt: "Points joined by a line, observed rate against mean predicted probability, with a dashed diagonal. The points lie close to the diagonal, most of them at predicted probabilities below 0.25."
#| classes: on-light
alt_text_holds(gap[best] < 0.05 and (cal_best["mean_predicted"] < 0.25).sum() > len(cal_best) / 2,
               "fig-results-calibration")
with style():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize(4.6, 4.2))
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color=MUTED, linewidth=1)
    ax.plot(cal_best["mean_predicted"], cal_best["observed_rate"], marker="o", color=ACCENT)
    top_value = max(cal_best["mean_predicted"].max(), cal_best["observed_rate"].max()) * 1.1
    ax.set_xlim(0, top_value)
    ax.set_ylim(0, top_value)
    ax.set_xlabel("Mean predicted probability")
    ax.set_ylabel("Observed subscription rate")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

For `{python} best`, no bin is more than `{python} f"{100 * gap[best]:.1f}"` percentage points
from the diagonal; for the oldest release, `{python} oldest`, the largest gap is
`{python} f"{100 * gap[oldest]:.1f}"`. The report says which release is best calibrated with a
guard, because that word, unlike the numbers, does not follow the data by itself.

When both documents render, review the branch as in @sec-fast-pr: the scope (`model-card.qmd`,
`references.bib`, `report.qmd`, perhaps `AGENTS.md`), one number against `outputs/`, and a
fresh clone. Then commit.

## Change a setting, explain the rebuild {#sec-results-change}

The call centre has room for more calls, so `TOP_SHARE` in `src/acme_eval/metrics.py`, the
share of the list that is called, can double. No prompt is supplied: this is the test of the
design, and you can do it by hand.

::: tryit
1. **Predict.** Before you double `TOP_SHARE`, write down which numbers in the report and the
   card will change, which will not, and whether anything will stop the render.
2. **Rebuild**: double it, run `uv run python scripts/evaluate.py`, render both documents.
3. **Undo**: `git restore` the file, then evaluate and render again.

::: done
you can name what changed, what did not and what stopped.
:::
:::

::: think
What should change, what should not, and what is the trap?

The number of calls (to `{python} f"{calls_double:,}"`) and every top-of-list metric change:
recall, precision, lift, each band's share called. ROC AUC, the Brier score (the mean squared
error of the probabilities) and the calibration do not: they describe the whole list, not
where it is cut. The trap is the share named in words: a typed "top 10%" stays. In the
finished project both documents stop on a caption's guard, and two unit tests that pin the
rule fail, on purpose.
:::

::: story
<!-- source: REVISION-PLAN.md line 475 (WP5) and results.qmd lines 272-277 at 651db10. They
disagree on whose report it was, so the story says only what both record. -->
When this change was tested for the book, with the list doubled, "top 10%" was still typed
in labels and a caption, beside the new figures. The numbers had moved and the words had
not. The labels compute the share now, and each caption that names it has a guard. After
you change a setting, search every output for its old value in words.
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- One script computes every result once into plain files; every document reads them, so a
  reviewer can trust that the report and the card quote the same run.
- Tests check the code and the data, guards check the prose, and the render checks the
  references; none of them sees a typed label, which a prediction and a rebuild do.
- A model card has a fixed set of sections, which is the vocabulary to ask for; its slices are
  where a model's effect on people shows.
- Hand an agent a larger task with a plan first, then judge the result by its guards, its
  references, its list of what it could not verify, and the render.
- Numbered sections and labelled tables and figures give references that resolve in every
  format; `citeproc: true` makes a Typst PDF cite like the others.
:::

The project now has two documents for readers who read. The next readers will be in a meeting,
in front of a screen.
